A Guide to Analyzing the Survey of Consumer Finances

SCF Package Team

Source: vignettes/SCF-guide.Rmd
SCF-guide.Rmd

Overview

The scf package provides a coherent framework for analyzing the Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF), a nationally representative, multiply-imputed survey of U.S. household wealth and income.

SCF data is analytically complex due to:

  • Multiple imputation (5 implicates per household)
  • Replicate weights (999 per implicate)
  • Oversampling of high-wealth households

This vignette introduces a complete workflow: downloading, loading, transforming, summarizing, modeling, and visualizing SCF data using Rubin’s Rules.

1. Installation and Setup 

install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("jncohen/scf")

Load the package:

library(scf)
library(survey)  # required backend

2. Downloading SCF Data 

scf_download(2022)

This creates a flat .rds file (scf2022.rds) containing all five implicates, merged with replicate weights.

3. Loading SCF Data 

scf2022 <- scf_load(2022)

This returns a svyimputationList object — a list of replicate-weighted designs ready for analysis.

4. Updating and Subsetting Data

Create new variables across all implicates:

scf2022 <- scf_update(scf2022,
  senior = age >= 65,
  log_income = log(income + 1)
)

Subset the dataset:

working_age <- scf_subset(scf2022, age >= 25 & age <= 64)

5. Descriptive Statistics

Mean 

scf_mean(scf2022, ~income)
scf_mean(scf2022, ~networth, by = ~edcl)

Median 

scf_median(scf2022, ~networth)

Percentile 

scf_percentile(scf2022, ~networth, q = 0.9)

Correlation 

scf_corr(scf2022, ~income, ~networth)

Cross-tabulation 

scf_xtab(scf2022, ~edcl, ~racecl, percent = "row")

6. Regression Models

OLS 

scf_ols(scf2022, income ~ age + factor(edcl))

Logistic Regression 

scf2022 <- scf_update(scf2022, rich = networth > 1e6)
scf_logit(scf2022, rich ~ age + factor(edcl), odds = TRUE)

Generalized Linear Models 

scf_glm(scf2022, hborrff ~ networth + factor(edcl), family = binomial())

To return odds ratios:

glm_out <- scf_glm(scf2022, hborrff ~ networth + factor(edcl), family = binomial())
exp(glm_out$pooled$results)

7. Visualization

Univariate (Discrete) 

scf_plot_dbar(scf2022, ~edcl)

Customize the plot:

scf_plot_dbar(scf2022, ~edcl,
  title = "Education of Household Head",
  xlab = "Education Level",
  fill = "steelblue"
)

Univariate (Continuous) 

scf_plot_hist(scf2022, ~age, bins = 10, fill = "steelblue")

Bivariate (Discrete–Discrete) 

scf_plot_bbar(scf2022, ~edcl, ~racecl, percent_by = "row")

Bivariate (Continuous–Discrete) 

scf_plot_cbar(scf2022, ~networth, ~edcl, stat = "median")
scf_plot_cbar(scf2022, ~networth, ~racecl, stat = 0.9)

Bivariate (Continuous–Continuous) 

scf_plot_scatter(scf2022, ~income, ~networth, method = "lm")

8. Extracting Implicate-Level Estimates

Most functions store implicate-level results as an attribute:

result <- scf_mean(scf2022, ~income)
scf_implicates(result)

This is useful for inspecting variation across imputations.

9. Learn More

  • SCF project site: https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/scfindex.htm
  • Codebooks for each wave available from the Fed
